prize_parts.citation: For empirical evidence on how import competition and technological change reshape local labour markets, employment and wages, and on the adjustment costs borne by workers and regions.

statement.case_for: My laureate set is unchanged from round 1: B036 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. What changed in round 2 is the scope of the citation and my second alternative. The case is a first-order question (who bears the adjustment costs of trade and technology) answered with transparent local-labour-market designs. Those designs have been replicated, challenged on shift-share identification, exposure measurement and persistence, and refined for about a decade. The central finding that exposure produced concentrated and lasting local adjustment costs has survived in qualified form. The credit is the most precise available on this ballot: the empirical programme is jointly authored by the three named people. I now drop 'wage inequality' and 'labour demand' from my wording. Those phrases would pull the citation toward the skill-premium and task strand, where credit is diffuse and overlaps with the 2023 and 2024 prizes. A citation about exposure, employment, wages and adjustment credits what the three can be shown to have done, and does not state an effect size. My design-based and cross-disciplinary reading of this work is consistent with how I framed the 2020 prize, but it is not independent evidence of merit. I do not treat the seven-of-eleven count as evidence of merit. Several of those supporters, including me, moved during round 1, so I have tested my own view against the strongest objections. I find the case for the trade-shock evidence holds on attribution and maturity. My remaining doubts concern magnitude and scope, and I do not think they defeat it.
statement.case_against: The long-run magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the shift-share exposure instruments behind them, are still contested. If the Committee judged this a contested estimate rather than a lasting discovery, the case would weaken. A trade-shock-centred trio leaves Katz and the task and skill-bias lineage uncredited, and originators outside the credited set (Acemoglu, recognised in 2024, and Levy and Murnane) are not named. The 2021 and 2023 labour prizes and the 2024 technology and institutions prize are thematically adjacent. Autor spans both strands, but the combined ballot item is not a single cleanly framed achievement, which is why the citation is narrower than the entry. B034 has tighter two-person credit and no comparable debate over magnitudes. If its Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority question could be settled, that would be a serious competing case. I cannot settle it from the supplied evidence.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B036 seventh and doubts the maturity bar. He cites continuing debate on identification, persistence and the magnitude of the China shock, and the overlap with Acemoglu's recognised work on tasks. He also says he would not oppose B036.
responses.response: I take the maturity doubt seriously and have changed the wording because of it. The citation now credits evidence on exposure, employment, wages and adjustment, and says nothing about elasticities or long-run aggregate size. The disagreement is about magnitude and persistence. It is not about whether the original finding was real, and the finding has been through about a decade of critique. I would not call every unresolved size debate a bar to maturity. Prizes have recognised discoveries while the estimates stayed contested. The task-framework overlap with Acemoglu is real, and it is the reason I dropped the 'wage inequality' language and kept the citation away from task theory. A finding that would change my view is a re-analysis showing that the employment and wage effects vanish under the main alternative exposure measures. I do not read the critiques I know of that way. That judgment rests on my own knowledge and is not independently verified.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B034 with Helpman and Melitz. She argues it is mature, has tight attribution to a two-person credit, and, unlike B036, has no comparable dispute about magnitudes or adjacent recent prize. She treats the Bernard et al. work as largely empirical and not a competing claim to the selection model.
responses.response: B034 is the strongest competing case, and I have moved it into my alternatives in place of B003 because of it. I agree the maturity and the two-name structure are clean. I am less sure that no adjacent prize exists, because the 2008 trade prize bears on it. Strömberg calls the priority question involving Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum his most serious reservation, and I cannot settle it either. That open question is why I keep B036 first. In B036 the dispute is about magnitudes, and the authorship of the central finding is not in question. In B034 the dispute is about who first established the mechanism and how it relates to the prior prize. I would not oppose B034 on scientific grounds if the Committee can draft a citation that separates selection across firms from the earlier work.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers B034. He says he would now propose Autor, Dorn and Hanson if B036 were preferred. He also acknowledges B036 as the strongest alternative, and he regards the magnitude and persistence debate as a reason to keep B034 ahead.
responses.response: We agree on the attribution, and your move off the Autor-Katz pairing supports the trio. We differ on how much the magnitude debate should weigh. I think it argues for careful wording, not for deferral. A reasonable test is whether the central finding survives the main critiques, and the follow-up work on persistence and adjustment refined it more than it reversed it. I accept your point that B034's credit structure is tidier on paper. But tidy credit that depends on an unsettled priority question is not clearly stronger than clear credit with a magnitude debate. I would want the Committee to put that comparison on the table directly, using the same maturity and attribution criteria for both.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B018 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He treats B036 as a close alternative. He argues the framework is four decades old and has been tested through the financial crisis and the 2021-23 inflation, with little overlap with the 2022 prize.
responses.response: I ranked B018 first at the opening, so I take this case seriously, and I agree on the division of credit among Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. I also agree that the 2021-23 inflation and heterogeneous-agent work extend the framework more than they displace it. My difficulty is still that any three-name cut omits Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, whose work made the framework operational. Whether the third name is Taylor or Galí is unresolved. A prize should be able to defend its credited set as the founding contribution and not as an arbitrary cut. I keep B018 as my first alternative. If the Committee found a trio it could defend, I would support it, and I do not regard the attribution cost as a reflection on the importance of the work.

responses.point: Hassler, as chair, moved to B036 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. He argues the citation should be anchored on the empirical evidence about trade and labour-market adjustment, not a general theory of technology. He also says the task framework has originators outside the entry.
responses.response: I agree, and my revised citation follows that anchoring. It names import competition and technological change as exposures whose effects on local labour markets, employment and wages were measured. It does not claim the theory of tasks. On the chair's question about trade-first versus technology-first wording, I prefer trade-first with technology as a second exposure. I would not name wage inequality in the citation, because that phrase invites the skill-premium strand. I also note your B010 alternative and Boppart's disclosure of collaboration with Klenow. I take no view on those ties. I am not relying on either member's ranking of B010.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee reads the trade-shock evidence as a lasting discovery or as a contested estimate, given the continuing shift-share and persistence debate. A convincing re-analysis under alternative exposure measures could change my view.

Whether leaving Katz and the task lineage uncredited, including originators outside the credited set, is an acceptable attribution cost, and whether a citation that names technological change can avoid implying more than it credits.

Whether B034's priority question involving Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and its overlap with the 2008 prize, can be resolved well enough to make it the stronger candidate. I cannot resolve this from the supplied evidence.
Whether a defensible three-name B018 credit exists. That depends on Taylor versus Galí as the third name and on how much weight the post-2008 and 2021-23 record carries.
My assessment relies on my own knowledge of the literature and on the supplied committee materials, with no independent verification of attribution claims.
statement.conflict_note: No personal tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz or any candidate on the alternatives B018 and B034 is apparent from my supplied profile. My ties are collegial: SSE affiliation alongside committee members Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg, and long-time Lund and market-design co-authors who do not appear on these ballot items. My field is market and mechanism design, which is distant from labour and trade, and I disclose that I gave the 2020 presentation speech and favoured cross-disciplinary empirical work there. Those speeches may reflect collective drafting and do not establish my private preferences. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated. I have no additional disclosure to add about colleagues' ties beyond those already recorded in the chair summary.
